title: One Broken Cable, Hundreds of Flights Cancelled: America's Air Traffic System Is 40 Years Old
summary:
Have you ever been stuck at an airport while your flight gets cancelled? Now imagine hundreds of flights cancelled at once — all because of one broken cable.

On Monday morning, a communications switch failed at the air traffic control center in Philadelphia. Controllers tried to switch to the backup line. But railroad construction workers had accidentally cut that line too. So for hours, controllers had no radar and no radios.

What happened next? No commercial flights landed at Newark airport from about 9:40 a.m. until just after 5:20 p.m. More than 200 flights were cancelled at Philadelphia International Airport. LaGuardia and Kennedy airports in New York were also disrupted. By Tuesday, nearly 100 more flights were cancelled because planes and crews were in the wrong places.

This isn't the first time. Similar outages happened in Minneapolis and Dallas in the past year. And in spring 2025, the same Philadelphia facility lost radar several times.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says the problem is simple: the system is 40 years old. 'This is a 40-year-old architecture or design,' he said. Congress already gave the FAA $12.5 billion to fix things. Now Duffy wants $20 billion more.

The good news? The controllers kept everyone safe. Their union said they did an 'exceptional job' even when their equipment failed.
why_it_matters: Many families fly for holidays and visits, so old equipment in one control room can suddenly cancel plans for thousands of people at once.

background_read: The FAA (the Federal Aviation Administration) is the US government group that organises the sky and sets the safety rules for flying.
Air traffic controllers sit in control rooms and talk to pilots by radio, telling them where to go so planes never crash into each other.
Radar was developed in the years before World War II, and controllers still rely on it to 'see' planes that are far away in clouds or darkness.
Article_Structure: WHO: Air traffic controllers in Philadelphia, railroad construction workers who cut a line, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, the FAA, Congress and the controllers' union.

WHAT: One broken communications switch — plus a backup line that was accidentally cut — left controllers without radar or radios, so hundreds of flights were cancelled and Newark stopped landing planes for hours.
WHERE: The air traffic control center in Philadelphia, affecting Philadelphia International, Newark, LaGuardia and Kennedy airports in New York.
WHY: Because the system is about 40 years old, similar outages have already happened in Minneapolis and Dallas, and fixing it needs billions of dollars.

perspectives.description: It says the controllers did an 'exceptional job' and kept everyone safe even when their radar and radios stopped working.
They were stranded and lost money, and they want the system fixed so one broken cable can't cancel hundreds of flights again.
Sean Duffy says the real problem is a 40-year-old design, and he is asking for $20 billion more after Congress already gave the FAA $12.5 billion.
